title: Latency to business outcomes — positioning brief
content:
Purpose:
This brief is an internal one-pager to help sales, product marketing, and field engineers explain Redwood’s core differentiator in customer conversations: turning predictable inference performance (latency and tail behavior) into measurable business outcomes.

One‑line thesis:
For engineering teams building LLM-powered features, Redwood turns inference unpredictability into a stable lever — letting teams ship high-quality, low-latency experiences that scale without obscene cost or operational debt.

Why this angle now:
- Customers increasingly choose technology based on SLOs not models. Fast models are table stakes; predictable latency across load and locations is what unblocks product launches.
- The cost/latency tradeoffs are now the primary gating factor for feature adoption (not model accuracy alone).
- Competitors emphasize model breadth or self-hosting; few give engineers a concise contract: “we guarantee the latency behavior you need, and we make it inexpensive.”

Customer problems we solve (plain language):
- "My chat feature works in dev but stalls under real traffic." (unreliable tail latency)
- "We can’t offer synchronous features because token costs spike unpredictably." (cost volatility)
- "We don’t have the expertise to tune batching/kv-cache while keeping SLA." (ops debt)

Redwood promise (short):
Ship LLM features that stay fast and cheap in production.

Core pillars (how we deliver the promise):
1) Predictable latency SLOs — routing, autoscaling, and fallback model variants that avoid surprise p50/p95/p99 regressions.
2) Cost-stable serving — batching, prefix/KV caching, and quantization guidance tied to real workload profiles.
3) Unified experience — same API/rollouts/observability across hosted, dedicated, private so teams don’t rewrite infra as they scale.
4) Developer ergonomics — quick SDKs, templates, and an operations console with token‑level cost breakdowns that non‑infra teams can act on.

Proof points for field use (talk tracks and data hooks):
- Benchmark: median p99 tail reduction vs baseline setup — e.g., “We cut p99 tail by 3–6x on customer X’s dialog workload via KV caching + smart routing.” (link to benchmark PR)
- Case vignette: marketplace customer who moved synchronous recommendations from async because of consistent 200–400ms tails after Redwood rollouts.
- Economic example: batching + cache reduced token spend by 28% in a mid‑sized SaaS app without degrading quality metrics.

Competitive differentiators (quick contrasts):
- Vs. model-only APIs: they sell models; we sell the whole contract — latency SLAs, rollback policies, and rollout tooling. Emphasize operational guarantees.
- Vs. self-host runtimes: self-host gives control but not the turnkey observability, rollout tooling, or cross-region capacity Redwood provides. We convert raw control into predictable outcomes.
- Vs. infrastructure vendors: they optimize kernels/hardware; we connect those optimizations to product-level SLOs and developer workflows so teams don’t need separate teams for serving/eval/ops.

Messaging hooks by buyer persona:
- Backend/ML Platform: “Make inference repeatable — same API and SLOs across environments, fewer runbooks and less toil.”
- Product/PM: “Ship features with latency SLAs you can promise customers without hiring a daemon ops team.”
- Engineering Lead/CTO: “Lower total cost of ownership for LLM features with predictable tails and fallback strategies.”

Quick objection handling (short bullets):
- "Why not just tune our own infra?" -> Tuning is brittle and specialized. We combine runtime engineering, operational playbooks, and product tooling so you get outcomes, not one-off tweaks.
- "How do we know quality won’t suffer if you optimize for cost/latency?" -> We tie quality monitoring to prompt/eval sets and provide regression alerts; rollouts can be canaryed against quality metrics.

Practical field checklist (things to surface in demos / POCs):
- Show p95/p99 heatmaps during synthetic burst tests.
- Walk through a canary rollback and automatic fallback to a CPU-safe model.
- Show token-level and route-level cost breakdown for a real-ish prompt set.
- Demo the autoscaling/burst config and how it maps to business targets (e.g., 99th percentile below X ms).

Open questions / To iterate:
- What explicit SLO templates do legal/sales need for contracts? (work with sales_ops)
- What standard prompt sets should we include in the demo kit for the top three verticals? (GTM to decide)
- Can we codify a simple ROI calculator for demos (input: users/hour, average tokens/req, desired p99) to show potential cost savings live?

Suggested CTAs for collateral & next steps:
- Build a one‑pager “Latency ROI calculator” widget for demo pages.
- Create three verticalized demo prompt sets (marketplaces, search, agent assistants).
- Produce a short playbook for SEs: 5 slides + 2-minute demo checklist aligned to this narrative.

Notes to self / shorthand for writers:
- Avoid heavy model claims; focus on service guarantees and developer outcomes.
- Use simple metrics in GTM: p99 tail, tokens-per-response, cost-per-1000-requests.
- Keep technical depth for SRE/Platform collateral; keep commercial pitch outcome-focused.

Attachments / references (linked artifacts above):
- See benchmarking PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/pull/67
- Internal Confluence page for demo assets: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/INF-gtm-anchors

End of brief.
